label: Our own pool
fact: More than 70% of children who die in a pool or spa drown at a home.
checks: Walk away from the pool gate. Does it close and latch by itself?
Pull each door to the pool almost shut. Does the alarm still sound?
Say out loud who the Water Watcher is before anyone gets in.
linkText: Fence it on all four sides

label: Grandma’s or a friend’s
fact: Grandparents’, neighbors’ and friends’ pools count too. More than 70% of children who die in a pool or spa drown at a home, including the homes of family, friends and neighbors.
checks: Find every pool, hot tub and pond before the kids do.
Pack a portable door alarm, and put it on the door to the water.
Agree who watches after swim time ends. That’s when kids wander back.

label: No pool here
fact: Most child drownings inside the home happen in the bathtub, and a toddler can drown in as little as an inch or two of water.
checks: Stay within arm’s reach at bath time. If you have to step away, take the baby with you.
Empty buckets, coolers and kiddie pools, and flip them over.
Put a latch on the toilet lid.

label: Lake, river or beach
fact: Water colder than 70°F can make anyone gasp and lose control of their breathing.
checks: A U.S. Coast Guard-approved life jacket on every child, fitted by weight, even on shore.
Swim where there’s a lifeguard. Where there isn’t, you are the lifeguard.
Keep kids out of cold water, and keep boots and coats in mind: they soak up water fast.

label: A party or holiday
fact: Adam slipped out during graduation week, with family in from out of town and nobody expecting him anywhere near the pool.
checks: Name a Water Watcher out loud, and hand the job off every 15 minutes.
Keep watching through cleanup and fireworks, when floaties come off.
When company leaves, check that doors, gates and alarms are still set.
